content: Epilepsy is a prevalent neurological condition that affects approximately 50 million individuals globally. Among these, nearly one-third experience epilepsy that cannot be adequately managed with a single antiepileptic drug (AED). These patients often require a combination of two or more AEDs to control their seizures. In recent years, several newer AEDs have been explored as adjunctive treatments for focal epilepsy, and losigamone is one such drug. This systematic review focuses on losigamone as an add-on therapy for focal epilepsy and serves as an update to a Cochrane Review initially published in 2012 and later updated in 2018. The primary objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and tolerability of losigamone when used as an adjunctive treatment for focal epilepsy. For the most recent update, conducted on August 20, 2019, a comprehensive search was performed across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Register of Studies (CRS Web), MEDLINE, PubMed, Embase, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP). No language restrictions were applied. Additionally, previous searches included trial registries, and the authors contacted the manufacturer of losigamone and study authors for supplementary information. The review included randomized controlled trials that compared losigamone with a placebo as an add-on therapy for focal epilepsy. Two independent reviewers assessed the quality of the studies and extracted data. The primary outcomes were a reduction in seizure frequency by 50% or more and complete seizure freedom. Secondary outcomes included treatment withdrawal and adverse events. Results were expressed as risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) or 99% CIs for specific adverse events to account for multiple testing. Two studies, involving a total of 467 participants aged over 18 years, met the inclusion criteria. Both studies evaluated losigamone at doses of 1200 mg/day or 1500 mg/day as an adjunctive therapy for focal epilepsy. One study was deemed to have good methodological quality, while the other was of uncertain quality. In terms of efficacy, the results demonstrated that participants receiving losigamone were significantly more likely to achieve a 50% or greater reduction in seizure frequency compared to those receiving a placebo (RR 1.76, 95% CI 1.14 to 2.72; moderate-quality evidence). However, losigamone was also associated with a significantly higher rate of treatment withdrawal compared to placebo (RR 2.16, 95% CI 1.28 to 3.67; moderate-quality evidence). Regarding tolerability, the proportion of participants experiencing adverse events was higher in the losigamone group than in the placebo group (RR 1.34, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.80; moderate-quality evidence). Dizziness was the only adverse event significantly associated with losigamone use (RR 3.82, 99% CI 1.69 to 8.64; moderate-quality evidence). Neither study reported the proportion of participants achieving complete seizure freedom. A subgroup analysis based on losigamone dosage revealed that a higher dose (1500 mg/day) was associated with a greater reduction in seizure frequency compared to a lower dose (1200 mg/day). However, the higher dose was also linked to an increased rate of treatment withdrawal due to adverse events. In conclusion, the findings of this review indicate that losigamone, when used as an add-on therapy for focal epilepsy, can reduce seizure frequency but is associated with a higher likelihood of treatment withdrawal and adverse events. The included studies were of short duration and uncertain quality, highlighting the need for future well-designed, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials with longer follow-up periods. No new studies were identified since the previous version of this review, and the overall quality of the evidence was judged to be moderate.
